Fluttereth
FLUT-ur-eth
v. (hovers with beating wings; of the eagle over her young, and so of the LORD over Israel)
From Old English floterian, to float or flap. At Deuteronomy 32:11 it renders Hebrew rachaph, to brood or hover — the same verb used of the Spirit of God moving upon the face of the waters.

Biblical Definition

The Song of Moses reaches for the one picture that will hold the whole wilderness history: As an eagle stirreth up her nest, fluttereth over her young, spreadeth abroad her wings, taketh them, beareth them on her wings: So the LORD alone did lead him, and there was no strange god with him. Four verbs in order, and every one of them matters. She stirs up the nest — breaks up the comfort, makes the young leave. She flutters over them, hovering while they fall. She spreads her wings. She takes them and bears them. The disturbance and the catching are the same bird, and the whole of it is called leading.

The Hebrew verb behind fluttereth is rachaph, which occurs only three times in the Old Testament, and its most famous use is Genesis 1:2, where the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters. The same brooding hover that was over the unformed creation is over the young eagles and over Israel in the desert. Moses had already used the image at Sinai — I bare you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto myself — and Isaiah promises it forward to all who wait on the LORD: they shall mount up with wings as eagles. The point of the figure is the last clause of Deuteronomy 32:12: the LORD alone did lead him, and there was no strange god with him. No other bird was involved.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): moves the wings rapidly; hovers; flaps the wings without flying away.

expand to see more

FLUTTER, v.i. To move or flap the wings rapidly, without flying, or with short flights; to hover.

HOVER, v.i. To hang over or about, fluttering with the wings; to hang about; to move to and fro near a place.

EAGLE, n. A rapacious fowl of the genus Falco, remarkable for strength, size, flight and longevity.

NEST, n. The place or bed formed or used by a bird for incubation or the mansion of her young.

BROOD, v.i. To sit on and cover, as a fowl on her eggs; to remain a long time in anxiety.

Key Scripture

Deuteronomy 32:11 — "As an eagle stirreth up her nest, fluttereth over her young, spreadeth abroad her wings, taketh them, beareth them on her wings:"

Deuteronomy 32:12 — "So the LORD alone did lead him, and there was no strange god with him."

Exodus 19:4 — "Ye have seen what I did unto the Egyptians, and how I bare you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto myself."

Isaiah 40:31 — "But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint."

Modern Corruption

God's care is imagined as the absence of disturbance, when the eagle in Moses' figure begins by breaking up the nest.

expand to see more

The figure is usually quoted from the middle — borne up on eagles' wings — and the first verb is left out. As an eagle stirreth up her nest: she wrecks the comfortable place deliberately, because young that are never made to leave will never fly. Israel's wilderness was that stirring, and Moses is telling them so at the end of forty years. A believer who defines God's kindness as the absence of upheaval has taken one verb out of a sequence of five and will not recognize the hand that is actually leading him.

The hovering is the other half and must not be lost either. Rachaph, the verb behind fluttereth, is the brooding of the Spirit over the deep in Genesis 1 — a hovering that produces order out of what has no form. The same God who empties the nest is underneath the falling bird with His wings out. And the clause that closes the figure guards it from becoming sentimental: the LORD alone did lead him, and there was no strange god with him. Whatever the wilderness looked like at the time, there was never a second explanation for it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew rachaph (H7363), to brood or hover; nesher (H5404), an eagle; ur (H5782), to stir up or rouse.

expand to see more

Hebrew rachaph (H7363) — to hover, to brood; used of the Spirit of God upon the face of the waters.

Hebrew ur (H5782) — to rouse, to stir up; what the eagle does to her nest first.

Hebrew nesher (H5404) — the eagle; the figure Moses uses of the LORD in the wilderness.

Hebrew paras (H6566) — to spread out; of the wings under the falling young.

Hebrew nasa (H5375) — to lift, to bear; the last of the five verbs, and the one Israel remembered.

Usage

"“As an eagle stirreth up her nest” — the verb usually left out."

"“fluttereth over her young” — the same word as the Spirit over the deep."

"“the LORD alone did lead him” — no second explanation for the wilderness."
